newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian politicians gird for battle over budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian politicians gird for battle over budget.

text.p: India's minority government and its reluctant partner the Congress Party began separate meetings on Friday to thrash out strategy ahead of a looming showdown over the nation's budget.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fragile United Front coalition is expected to call parliament's budget session on February 20, officials said.
Analysts said the uneasy alliance between Deve Gowda and Congress President Sitaram Kesri could hit a flashpoint in debate over the budget for fiscal 1997/98 ending March 31.
But Congress, which was ejected from power by the United Front following general elections in May last year, was careful not to take an openly confrontational stand.
"This is not a meeting to decide if the Congress will or will not withdraw its support to Deve Gowda," one Congress official told Reuters.
"We have to brief our members of parliament about what we think of our support to the government so far."

Former Congress finance minister Manmohan Singh, who masterminded a dramatic liberalisation of India's economy in the early 1990s, will assess the United Front's performance at a meeting of his party's parliamentarians, officials said.
Singh has accused the United Front of mishandling the radical reforms he initiated in 1991 and triggering a slowdown in economic growth.

Industrial growth slowed to 9.8 percent in April-September 1996 compared with 12.1 percent a year earlier. Inflation, measured by the wholesale price index, hit 7.75 percent on January 4, a 58-week high.
The Planning Ministry estimates gross domestic product growth in 1996/97 will slow to 6.5 percent after 7.1 percent the previous year.
The economy could be overshadowed by a simmering row over corruption, Congress officials said.
On January 21 Switzerland handed India secret bank documents linked to an arms scandal involving the sale of Swedish artillery after seven years of legal wrangling in Swiss courts.
India's Central Bureau of Investigation has said the papers will allow a reopening of the case, which stems from India's $1.3 billion artillery deal with Sweden's AB Bofors in 1986.
India has been trying for years to determine if senior politicians took bribes in connection with the arms deal.
The furore contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government led by Congress prime minister Rajiv Gandhi.

Swiss police said there was evidence Bofors paid about $40 million into various banks accounts in Switzerland. Bofors has denied the payments were bribes and said the money represented settlement costs to its agents.
Government sources said Deve Gowda's troubled ties with Congress could worsen with the handing over of the documents.

Congress president Kesri has promised to cleanse the party of corruption. But his aides said he regards the reopening of the Bofors issue as an attempt by the United Front to tarnish Congress's image.
The United Front, on its part, is divided over several key reform measures like the opening up of the insurance, aviation and media sectors to foreign investors.
Deve Gowda is also faced with a political minefield over the issue of raising the prices of petroleum products, a move regarded by the government's economic advisers as long overdue.

Deve Gowda, with fewer than 200 supporters in the 545-seat Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament), needs the support of the 137 Congress deputies to beat off a relentless challenge from the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.
